overview: Gentrack is a New Zealand-headquartered, NZX/ASX dual-listed vertical software company that sells mission-critical billing, customer information system (CIS) and operational software to two very different end markets: energy and water utilities (via its "g2"/Velocity platform) and airports (via its Veovo brand, covering passenger flow, resource management and revenue systems). Revenue is earned mostly as multi-year recurring SaaS/support fees layered with lumpy, project-based non-recurring implementation and licence revenue, from roughly 60+ utility customers and 150+ airports across EMEA, APAC and, increasingly, the Americas and Middle East. The company suffered a near-death experience in FY2019–FY2021 (UK energy retailer collapses plus COVID grounding air travel) before rebuilding into a higher-margin, more diversified group through FY2022–FY2025.

business_model.summary: Gentrack licenses and hosts billing/CIS software for utilities (Utilities segment, ~84% of FY25 group revenue) and airport operations/passenger software for airports (Veovo segment, ~16% of FY25 group revenue). Revenue is split into recurring revenue (Annual/CMRR software fees, Support Services/TRR, and Managed Services — 60-67% of group revenue and growing) and non-recurring revenue (NRR: implementation projects, licences, and for Veovo, hardware sales — lumpy and dependent on the timing of new customer go-lives and upgrades). Long implementation cycles (roughly 6+ months from contract to first go-live, sometimes multi-year for large Tier-1 deployments) create revenue lumpiness quarter to quarter but underpin very sticky, multi-year recurring contracts once live.
business_model.customer_type: B2B enterprise — large regulated utility retailers/networks and major international airports and air navigation service providers, multi-year contracts
business_model.geographic_mix: FY25 Utilities revenue: EMEA ~$111.7m (58%) vs APAC ~$81.7m (42%), with EMEA (chiefly UK) growing 13% YoY while APAC was flat. Veovo revenue is spread across EMEA, Americas and APAC, with the DTP (Dubai Technology Partners) acquisition in May 2026 adding Middle East depth.

competitive_position.market_position: A mid-sized, focused challenger in two separate niche verticals — not the scale leader in either. In utilities CIS/billing it competes as a more configurable, cloud-native alternative to legacy SAP/Oracle stacks and against the fast-growing Kraken platform (Octopus Energy's in-house-built tech, now spun out and licensed to third parties, reportedly serving 50-70m+ accounts across ~27 countries). In airports, Veovo is a mid-tier specialist behind larger integrated players such as Amadeus and SITA, competing on data/analytics depth (AODB, FIDS, passenger flow, resource management) rather than breadth.

moat_factors.description: Billing/CIS is mission-critical, regulator-facing infrastructure; migrations take 6-24+ months and carry major operational/compliance risk, making customers reluctant to re-platform once live (evidenced by multi-year implementation timelines and long-tenured top-10 customers).
CMRR/TRR/Managed Services contracts are multi-year and grew to ~$174m guided for FY26 (>10% growth), providing revenue visibility, though this is offset by customer-level concentration risk.

Deep knowledge of UK/EU and ANZ energy retail regulation, billing complexity and market-specific rules (e.g. UK Ofgem rules, water retail deregulation) is a barrier to new entrants without local expertise.

Gentrack is a challenger, not the incumbent, in both verticals; Kraken, SAP/Oracle in utilities and Amadeus/SITA in airports are all larger and better resourced, and Kraken in particular has shown it can win business from Gentrack's own installed base (e.g., Meridian Energy in NZ moved off its Gentrack-linked billing arrangement to Kraken in 2025).

weaknesses: Two-segment structure means neither business achieves the scale/network effects of a single-market leader
High revenue lumpiness from NRR/project timing makes near-term guidance unreliable (illustrated by the May 2026 guidance cut)

Kraken's rapid international expansion (backed by Octopus Energy and third-party licensing deals) is a credible, well-funded threat in the ANZ/UK retail energy markets that are core to Gentrack's Utilities base

g2.0/Velocity platform transition still maturing — first full-scope go-live (Genesis Energy) only completed in H1 FY26, so the new platform's win-rate and margin profile are not yet fully proven at scale
EBITDA margins (12% FY25, guided 6-9% FY26 including elevated investment) remain well below the 15-20% medium-term target and below typical SaaS peer margins

growth_drivers: g2.0/Velocity platform rollout — management says it is 'resonating' with both energy and (newly) water utilities and is central to the >15% medium-term revenue CAGR target
Water sector entry — Pennon Water Services (UK) signed as Gentrack's first major water utility customer, opening a new addressable market beyond energy retail

Pipeline maturity — as of FY25/H1 FY26, Gentrack cited being preferred vendor/shortlisted at up to 10 prospects representing ~30m meter points across EMEA and APAC, with 3-4 targeted wins through to March 2027

Veovo momentum — major new contracts (NAV Canada national billing platform, a Tier-1 Asian airport) and recurring revenue growth of ~18-33% YoY across recent periods; management describes the ex-hardware business as approaching a 'Rule of 50' profile

Bolt-on M&A — two acquisitions in May 2026 (Factor, an AI energy pricing/forecasting business, NZ$24m + earn-out; and DTP, an airport AI/messaging platform in the Middle East, NZ$17m) funded from Gentrack's debt-free cash balance, intended to add capability and accelerate market entry

AI-driven cost-to-serve reduction narrative for utility retailers (30-70% potential opex reduction cited by management) and rising complexity from the energy transition (distributed generation, EVs, smart meters) that increases the value of modern billing/pricing platforms
Geographic expansion into North America (Veovo's NAV Canada win) and further Middle East penetration via DTP
$20m on-market share buyback (up to 5% of shares on issue) announced May 2026, signalling capital return alongside growth investment

business.risk: Customer concentration and lumpy project revenue
business.description: Non-recurring/project revenue is inherently lumpy and dependent on the timing of a relatively small number of large implementation projects and go-lives; the FY26 guidance cut was driven largely by softer NRR and delayed new-customer wins, not recurring revenue.

Octopus Energy's Kraken platform is a well-capitalised, fast-growing competitor with tens of millions of managed accounts globally; it has demonstrated it can win against Gentrack-linked incumbents in Gentrack's core ANZ/UK markets (e.g., Meridian Energy in New Zealand moved to Kraken in 2025), creating both a competitive and reputational risk.

The new platform only achieved its first full-scope go-live (Genesis Energy) in H1 FY26; broader rollout, margin profile and win-rate at scale are still being proven, and elevated product investment is compressing near-term EBITDA margins.

Two acquisitions (Factor and DTP) were completed within weeks of each other in May 2026; integrating new teams, technology and go-to-market motions concurrently with a platform transition adds execution risk.

financial.description: Revenue and costs are earned across NZD, GBP, EUR, AUD and USD; reported results include material forex swings (e.g., $3.2m-$5.4m of intercompany forex gains in FY25 flattered NPAT and cash), which can reverse and obscure underlying trading performance.

Long-term incentive scheme accounting and associated tax treatment materially swings reported NPAT year to year (e.g., FY25 NPAT benefited from an LTI-related tax credit and lower LTI charges; H1 FY26 included a $2.1m reversal of prior LTI costs after an EPS hurdle was missed), making headline NPAT/EPS a noisy guide to underlying performance.

regulatory.risk: UK/EU energy retail regulation and supplier stability
regulatory.description: A meaningful share of Utilities revenue depends on the health and regulatory environment of UK/EU energy retailers; the FY2019-2021 wave of UK supplier failures previously wiped out a swathe of Gentrack's customer base and remains a structural tail risk if energy price volatility returns.
Expansion into UK water retail (Pennon) is a new regulatory domain (Ofwat rules) for Gentrack, distinct from its established energy expertise.

macro.description: Veovo's project/hardware revenue is tied to airport capital investment cycles and passenger volumes, which are cyclical and were severely impaired during COVID; a global travel downturn would again pressure this segment.

Utility customers' willingness to invest in new billing platforms is sensitive to energy price volatility and their own margin pressures; a severe energy-price shock could again destabilise smaller retail customers.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Utility software (CIS/billing) demand is underpinned by secular trends — energy market deregulation in new geographies, decarbonisation/electrification driving complexity (distributed generation, EVs, smart meters, dynamic pricing), and AI-driven cost-to-serve pressure on retailers moving off legacy mainframe systems. Airport software demand is recovering with global air travel growth and increasing airport investment in passenger experience/AI-driven operations technology (Veovo growing ~15-30% in recent periods).
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate. Recurring revenue (now >75% of group revenue) is relatively defensive, but non-recurring/project revenue and Veovo hardware sales are cyclical and tied to customer capex cycles and new-logo win timing, causing significant period-to-period lumpiness as demonstrated in FY26 guidance.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct exposure — Gentrack is debt-free with a net cash position (~NZ$73-85m through FY25/H1 FY26); indirect sensitivity comes via customers' capex appetite and equity market multiples applied to growth software names.
key_input_costs: Skilled software engineering/development talent (UK, NZ, offshore)
Sales & marketing investment to win new utility/airport logos

recent_developments.event: Stock remains well below its 2025 peak (~NZ$12) after the May 2026 sell-off; consensus analyst price targets and EPS estimates were cut materially following the guidance reset.

H1 FY26 (six months to 31 March 2026) results reported: group revenue $110.1m (down 1.7% YoY), recurring revenue up 12% to $85.3m, EBITDA excl. acquisition costs $7.9m (down from $13.0m), NPAT $5.1m (down from $7.2m), net cash $73.2m and no external debt. No interim dividend declared.

Announced two bolt-on acquisitions simultaneously: Factor (AI-driven energy pricing/forecasting technology for g2, enterprise value NZ$24m plus up to NZ$10m earn-out) and DTP/Dubai Technology Partners (AI-centric airport technology, expands Veovo's Middle East presence, reported ~NZ$17m), both funded from existing cash.

Cut FY26 revenue guidance to NZ$229-238m (from a prior ~NZ$250m-plus range) and flagged a weaker EBITDA outlook (guided NZ$13.5-20m excl. acquisition costs), citing softer non-recurring/project revenue and delayed new customer wins; simultaneously announced intention to launch an on-market share buyback of up to NZ$20m (up to 5% of shares on issue) over 12 months. Shares fell as much as ~34% in a single session on the news.
g2 platform went live for Genesis Energy, New Zealand's largest integrated energy company — Gentrack's first full-scope g2.0 deployment, a key proof point for the platform.

FY2025 annual results (year to 30 September 2025): group revenue up 8% to $230.2m (in line with guidance), recurring revenue up 13% to $155.4m, Utilities revenue up 7% to $193.4m, Veovo revenue up 15% to $36.8m (up 30% ex-hardware), EBITDA up 18% to $27.8m (12% margin), NPAT more than doubled to $20.9m (aided by a tax credit and FX gains), net cash $84.8m. Pennon Water Services signed as first major UK water customer; NAV Canada signed as Veovo's largest billing customer.
Invested a further NZ$4.9m in associate Amber Electric (total ~10% stake) as part of Amber's funding round, alongside the original NZ$12.9m investment made in January 2024.

New Zealand energy retailer Meridian Energy publicly moved its retail billing technology strategy to Kraken (Octopus Energy), impairing its in-house Flux platform — illustrating the competitive threat Kraken poses even within Gentrack's home ANZ market.

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 results and 5 May 2026 market update

items.notes: Cut on 5 May 2026 from prior guidance in the ~NZ$250m+ range, reaffirmed at H1 FY26 results on 18 May 2026; driven by softer non-recurring/project revenue and delayed timing of new customer wins.

items.target: Growth of more than 10% to approximately NZ$174m
items.notes: Non-recurring revenue explicitly guided to be lower than FY25 ($75m).
Down materially from FY25's $27.8m as the company prioritises growth investment (g2.0 rollout, sales/product spend) over near-term margin; LTI costs expected to be ~$2m higher in H2 FY26 than H1.
Reiterated at both FY25 results (Nov 2025) and H1 FY26 results (May 2026); contingent on converting 3-4 of the ~10 pipeline opportunities (c.30m meter points) through to March 2027.
Stated to be after expensing all development costs (i.e., not adjusted/capitalised R&D); expected to be reached as recurring revenue scales and operating leverage improves.

items.target: Cash generative before acquisitions and share buyback
items.notes: H1 FY26 cash outflow of $11.6m reflected normal first-half seasonality (payment of prior year bonuses/LTI taxes); management expects a working-capital inflow in H2 FY26.

items.target: On-market share buyback of up to NZ$20m (up to 5% of shares on issue)
items.notes: Funded from existing cash reserves; no interim FY26 dividend was declared.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Gary Miles has framed FY25 as a year of 'international pipeline development' with a return to higher revenue growth expected in FY26, though the actual H1 FY26 print and subsequent guidance cut show that pipeline conversion has been slower than expected, with management attributing the shortfall to deal complexity and buyer-side timing rather than competitive losses. Management continues to point to a mature, multi-region pipeline (c.30m meter points, ~10 opportunities) and reiterates confidence in the >15% CAGR / 15-20% EBITDA margin medium-term targets, while acknowledging it is 'too early' to provide FY27 guidance. CFO John Priggen has emphasised the group's debt-free, cash-generative balance sheet as the basis for both continued organic investment and the new buyback/bolt-on M&A capital allocation.

bull_case: Recurring revenue is genuinely growing well (up 12-13% in both FY25 and H1 FY26) and now represents roughly three-quarters of group revenue, a healthier mix than the headline growth-rate miss suggests

Debt-free balance sheet with net cash of ~NZ$73-85m gives Gentrack the flexibility to fund bolt-on M&A (Factor, DTP), invest through the platform transition, and run a NZ$20m buyback simultaneously without financial strain

g2.0/Velocity platform has now proven itself with a first full-scope go-live (Genesis Energy) and is winning in adjacent verticals (Pennon, the first water utility customer), opening a materially larger addressable market beyond energy retail

Veovo is executing well independent of the Utilities weakness — recurring revenue up 18-33% YoY, major new logos (NAV Canada, a Tier-1 Asian airport) and an approaching 'Rule of 50' profile ex-hardware

May 2026 sell-off (~34% single-day drop) may have overshot if the market mispriced a project-revenue timing issue as a structural growth/competitive failure, particularly given the maturing pipeline (c.30m meter points) management still points to
bear_case: Kraken is a credible, well-funded and expanding competitor that has already displaced Gentrack-linked technology at a marquee customer in Gentrack's home ANZ market (Meridian Energy), raising real doubts about Gentrack's ability to defend share as Kraken licenses its platform more broadly

FY26 guidance has already been cut once (revenue and EBITDA both lowered materially in May 2026) only months after FY25 results, denting confidence in management's forecasting and pipeline-conversion track record

EBITDA margins are guided to fall sharply in FY26 (to roughly 6-9%, well below FY25's 12% and the 15-20% medium-term target) as the company front-loads investment, meaning near-term earnings quality will likely stay weak and volatile

Non-recurring/project revenue remains a large, lumpy and hard-to-predict share of the business, and two concurrent acquisition integrations (Factor, DTP) completed within weeks of each other add execution risk on top of the ongoing g2.0 platform transition

Reported NPAT has been repeatedly flattered by one-off items (LTI-related tax credits, FX gains on intercompany loans, LTI cost reversals), so headline earnings and EPS may overstate underlying, sustainable profitability
